strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck: reducing inference latency of transformer-based diffusion policies for real-time robotic control.
The proposed BAC method is simple, training-free, and reasonably well motivated by observed temporal and block-wise feature similarity patterns.
The paper identifies and analyzes a nontrivial failure mode of naive block-wise caching, namely inter-block error propagation and FFN error surges, and proposes a concrete mitigation via BUA.
Empirical coverage is fairly broad: RoboMimic PH/MH, Push-T, Block Pushing, Kitchen, a real-world robot task, and an RDT-1B/VLA setting.
The main simulation results show strong speedups around 3x while often matching full-precision policy success rates, especially for S=10.
Appendices include useful ablations over n, similarity metrics, DDIM integration, and detailed cache schedules, which improves transparency.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental relative to existing diffusion caching work: the main contribution is an adaptation and scheduling refinement for diffusion policies rather than a fundamentally new acceleration paradigm.

The claim of 'lossless' acceleration is overstated. Several settings show noticeable degradation, especially aggressive caching, DDIM+BAC with small S, Tool Hang, Transport, and some MH/multi-stage cases.

The scheduler appears task/checkpoint dependent and relies on precomputed feature similarity or episode homogeneity; the cost, protocol, and robustness under distribution shift are not fully characterized.

Baseline comparison is incomplete. The paper compares mostly uniform caching, TeaCache adaptation, and DDIM, but does not deeply compare against broader robot-policy acceleration methods, model distillation, fewer-step samplers with tuned policies, or VLA-specific caching such as token-level methods.
Real-world validation is limited to one setup/task, with unclear number of trials and no statistical confidence intervals, making it hard to judge reliability under deployment variability.
The reported speedups mix FLOPs and measured speed, but kernel overhead, memory traffic, batching, and controller integration details are not analyzed enough to support general hardware claims.

The theoretical analysis explains first-order FFN error propagation, but it does not provide guarantees that BUA will select the right blocks or preserve policy quality; the argument remains mostly diagnostic.
Hyperparameters S and n have significant effects, and the selected defaults appear tuned per regime; the method may require nontrivial calibration to avoid collapses.
Reproducibility is only partial because the implementation is promised for future release, and some references/metadata look placeholder-like, which weakens polish and confidence.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: diffusion-policy inference latency is a real bottleneck for high-frequency robot control.

The paper identifies a plausible source of redundancy in transformer-based diffusion policies and proposes a training-free block-wise caching mechanism with a concrete scheduler and error-propagation heuristic.
The experimental section is broad in coverage, including RoboMimic, Push-T, Kitchen, Block Pushing, a real-world Franka setup, and an RDT-1B/ManiSkill experiment.
Ablations attempt to separate the contributions of adaptive scheduling and the Bubbling Union Algorithm, and the appendices include additional sensitivity studies and schedule visualizations.
weaknesses: The central claims are substantially overstated. Terms such as “lossless,” “for free,” and “readily integrable” are not justified: BAC often changes success rates, requires task-specific offline schedule computation, and depends on nontrivial hyperparameters such as S and n.

The scheduling objective is not fully convincing. The paper optimizes sums of consecutive feature similarities rather than directly measuring the error from reusing a cached feature over skipped timesteps, so the DP objective is only loosely connected to the claimed cache fidelity objective.

The method relies heavily on task-level episode homogeneity. This assumption is only empirically checked after the fact and may break under distribution shift, diverse language goals, multimodal behaviors, changing observations, or genuinely open-ended VLA deployment.

The real-world evaluation is hard to interpret. Full DDPM reportedly has extremely low success, while an approximate cached version succeeds much more often, which suggests the comparison is entangled with control frequency, latency, and action-chunk execution rather than isolating generation quality. The number of trials and statistical uncertainty are also unclear.

Baselines appear incomplete or potentially unfair. Important acceleration alternatives are either absent or only lightly adapted, and it is unclear whether DDIM, TeaCache, and uniform caching are tuned to comparable quality-speed tradeoffs.

Several reported results contradict the strong narrative: aggressive BAC settings collapse on difficult tasks, n and S require careful tuning, and appendix tables show severe failures for some settings despite claims of robustness.

The theory around FFN error propagation is mostly explanatory rather than predictive. The proposed Bubbling Union Algorithm is heuristic, and the paper does not provide a principled guarantee or a convincing analysis of when it will fail.

Reproducibility is limited. The project page is blank in the manuscript text, code is only promised for future release, and many implementation details needed to reproduce the offline schedule generation and real-world evaluation are underspecified.

Presentation quality is uneven, with typographical issues, vague claims, and some benchmark/task descriptions that appear inaccurate or imprecise, reducing confidence in the care of the empirical study.

strengths: Timely and practically important problem: reducing inference latency for transformer-based Diffusion Policy and diffusion-based VLA models is highly relevant for real-time robot control.
The proposed BAC framework is technically well motivated, combining a dynamic-programming adaptive caching scheduler with a targeted mechanism for mitigating inter-block error propagation.

The paper identifies and analyzes an interesting failure mode of naive block-wise caching, namely FFN-centered error surges, and supports the explanation with theory, correlation experiments, and visualizations.

Experimental coverage is strong: the evaluation includes real-world robot experiments, multiple simulation benchmarks, RoboMimic PH/MH settings, multi-stage tasks, Push-T, Kitchen, Block Pushing, and an RDT-1B VLA setting.
Results are convincing overall, with roughly 3x speedups while often preserving full-precision success rates, and meaningful improvements over uniform caching and an adapted TeaCache baseline.
Ablations are useful and directly test the main components, including ACS, BUA, the choice of similarity metric, and sensitivity to the upstream-block hyperparameter n.
The method is attractive as a training-free plugin, which increases practical adoption potential and distinguishes it from acceleration methods requiring retraining.
weaknesses: The claim of "lossless" acceleration is somewhat overstated: several settings show nontrivial degradation under more aggressive schedules or different hyperparameters, and the guarantees are empirical rather than formal.

BAC depends on task-specific offline schedule construction and an assumption of high episode homogeneity; although the appendix provides evidence, robustness to distribution shift, new tasks, different embodiments, or changing deployment conditions remains insufficiently explored.

The real-world evaluation is encouraging but narrow, focusing on one hardware setup and task; stronger statistical reporting, more trials, and more diverse real-world tasks would make the practical claims more compelling.

Baselines are reasonable but not exhaustive. The comparison to broader robotics/VLA acceleration methods, scheduler-based sampling reductions, token caching methods, and hardware-aware optimization could be more complete.

The theoretical analysis of error propagation is mainly local and explanatory; it does not provide a predictive criterion for when BUA will succeed or fail, nor does it tightly connect to downstream control success.

Reproducibility is not fully established at submission time because the implementation is promised for future release; exact schedule generation, calibration data requirements, and runtime overhead details should be easier to reproduce independently.

Some presentation choices are overly strong or slightly imprecise, including repeated "for free" and "lossless" phrasing despite offline calibration, hyperparameter tuning, and cases where performance drops occur.
